body_markdown:
Autumn brings crisper air and earlier sunsets. For a lot of us classic-car people, it also brings an emotional come-to-Jesus moment with ourselves. Or, perhaps more realistically, it’s our significant others who have it with us.


There’s a romantic *joie de vivre* in wrenching on a non-running jalopy under the hot July sun. Doing the same job in a parka, under a tarp that slaps you in the back every time the wind gusts, while rain whips sideways into your face on a gloomy November afternoon, is anything but.


“Maybe it’s time to sell the Galaxie,” you think, staring out the kitchen window with a mug of coffee in your hand. Cat and raccoon prints run up the hood and across the roof of the faded seafoam-green sedan.


proxibid/Grahams I-15 Auctions


You’re right. You aren’t going to get it running this year and, with Carla’s mother moving in next spring, there’s a good chance you never will. So you open the old laptop, pull up Facebook Marketplace and upload your favorite photos of the wayward sled—the ones from the day you towed it home from Walla Walla, when you had the whole world ahead of you.


The minute you hit publish, my phone buzzes with an alert that[a ’63 Galaxie](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ford/galaxie/1963) has been listed nearby. That’s when your woe gets interesting for me, because autumn is the best time of year to buy a project—and the closer it gets to the holidays, the better.


## Storage Math Is on Your Side


Unsplash/Roger Starnes Sr.


Most project owners don’t have a heated shop. They have a cramped garage, a driveway, a carport, or a rented storage unit that sends a bill every month whether anyone turns a wrench or not.


Hagerty contributor Jeff Zurschmeide is living this right now. He’s selling a 1972 VW Safari, the Mexican-market version of[the Thing](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/volkswagen/181_thing/1972/1972-volkswagen-181_thing-base?id=aCn1I000000DLUiSAO) , with the bus reduction-gear axles and raised ride height. It isn’t that he’s lost interest. He’s simply out of indoor space. “It’s super cool, but either it or[my Transporter](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/born-a-humble-workhorse-vws-original-bus-1950-67-is-a-prince-among-collector-cars/) would have to live outside for the winter, and I am not gonna let my Transporter get rust.” he says.


The calendar changes how sellers think about price. In June, car owners still believe they’re going to finish the thing, so they price it like the finished car they see in their head. They’re in no hurry, and they’re super-duper going to get it done by fall.


By November, that dream is gone. The summer slipped by without much progress. The days are short and wet, and a non-running car with no end in sight is costing them money every month. A seller who wouldn’t budge off their number in August will often take a lot less to make that bill go away before the holidays.


Don’t expect to find that in the price guides, though. Greg Ingold, editor of the Hagerty Price Guide, says the guide is built on nationwide averages. At that scale, he says, “we don’t track an appreciable difference or swing in values seasonally.” What changes is the pace. “If anything, we see a slowing of the market activity, but not always with value drops.”


Up close, it’s a different story. “In Northern Michigan where I live, it is absolutely harder to sell a project vehicle the closer the winter months approach,” Ingold says. “I know from firsthand experience.” A project’s book value may not budge in November, but the guy staring at a tarp and a storage bill often will.


At the same time, the buyer pool shrinks. Few casual shoppers want to tow a non-runner home in the rain, which leaves you competing with a handful of serious buyers, instead of a dozen dreamers.


Zurschmeide sees the same thing from the buying side, and he says the effect goes beyond projects. “Fall is the best time to buy convertibles (like the Safari) or sports cars,” he says. “People used them all summer and don’t want to or can’t stash them when the rain comes.” He’s eyeing a few well-kept six-cylinder BMW Z3 roadsters right now for exactly that reason.


## What “Ran Great When Parked” Really Means


Getty Images


The phrase tells you the engine ran at some point. It doesn’t tell you when, why it stopped, or what has happened to it since.


Years back, I stumbled on an ad for a classic car that included a description that went something like: “Ran great until it developed a knock and I parked it 10 years.” That one has stuck with me, because I never understood why the seller included the first part of that sentence. He might as well have just written “ran great when new.”


So, ask when it last ran, why it was parked, and whether it’s been kept inside. A seller who balks at those questions probably isn’t telling you the whole story.


If you’ve watched Hagerty’s *[Driveway Finds](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rdIAbr-EQ3k)* , you know an engine that turns over by hand won’t always run once it’s tuned up. Then again, John Brito and Dustin Hallinan have brought more classics back to life on old fuel and ancient oil than I ever would have wagered.


The cold works in your favor here, too. Combustion likes heat, and a warm afternoon can hide a hard start or smooth out a rough idle. Ask the seller not to start it before you show up—you’ll get a more honest read on the engine at 40 degrees than you ever would at 85. Just bring a towel if it’s raining, because wet paint always looks better than it is.


## Negotiate Like a Decent Person


Volvo


My first fall purchase was a project-condition[1974 Volvo 144](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/volvo/144/1974/1974-volvo-144-base?id=aCn1I000000DUA0SAO) , in November 2007. The seller’s wife had told him to get rid of it that spring, even though he was partway through the restoration. He told her he had. Then she visited him at work unannounced and found the car there. With nowhere else to put it and a fuming wife at home, he finally listed it for a quick sale.


He was asking $4000. I paid $3500, because I showed up with cash and could take it away that day. I worked at a Volvo shop at the time, too. So, he felt better knowing it was going to a good home, even if he took a hit on it.


Later that week, my boss and I swapped in an M41 overdrive four-speed I’d pulled from a ’75 244 at a Volvo junkyard. That was the only year the 240 used that gearbox. Before long, the 144 was ferrying me between the Volvo shop and journalism school with an improved transmission. I texted the seller telling him of my handiwork. He was genuinely psyched it was already getting cared for and improved.


## Spring, with a Running Car


Mecum


None of this works unless you actually spend the winter wrenching. So, make sure you’ve got covered space before you hand over the cash. Otherwise, the cycle repeats itself. The guy who buys a project in November with nowhere to put it is the guy who lists it next October, with his own favorite photos and his own “ran great when parked.”


Back to the Galaxie. If I bring it home in November, I’ve got four or five months of short days and long nights to sort the fuel system, rebuild the brakes, and find out whether that 390 really did run great when it was parked. Once it does, the seller’s getting a video.
